title: Andrews–Dyson-type partition identities as 'identities in growing families'
connection: Partition theory has infinite families of identities (Rogers–Ramanujan type) with growing parameters, proved by q-series. ES needs growing certificate families whose union covers all p; q-series identity machinery (Bailey chains) generates infinite families systematically.
why: Bailey-chain-style generators for ES identities (indexed by a growing parameter) would be a systematic way to produce non-B1 families.
first_step: Low priority; look for an ES identity family indexed by k with a recursive (chain) structure, e.g. from power ladders.

title: ES mod N: solvable for every N once denominators may share primes with n (no local obstruction)
connection: For every modulus N there are solutions of 4xyz ≡ n(xy + yz + zx) (mod N), but NOT always with x, y, z units: e.g. N = n = 5 forces 5 | xyz. Local solubility in the Bright–Loughran sense allows denominators divisible by primes of n (Type I/II at p).
why: Boundary marker: all content of ES is global; finite-field information enters only through densities (singular series). The 'units-only' local problem is obstructed at primes dividing n — the local shadow of 'p must divide a denominator'.
first_step: Record as lemma; compute the local densities at small primes for the singular series (items in batches B/E).

title: ES along thin exponential sequences: Fermat numbers are trivial, 4·3^k + 1 is not
connection: Thin sequences of special form often admit identities: n ≡ 2 (mod 3) is easy (4/n = 1/n + 1/((n+1)/3) + 1/(n(n+1)/3)), so Fermat numbers 2^{2^a} + 1 ≡ 2 (mod 3) are trivial; but n = 4·3^k + 1 ≡ 1 (mod 3) and ≡ 1 (mod 4) is not automatically easy. Systematically listing thin exponential families where ES is automatic vs hard.
why: Exponential families are where power-ladder certificates live; knowing which families are automatically easy narrows hard ones.
first_step: For families a·b^k + c with small a, b, c and p prime, test which have a uniform identity for all k (cf. Proth item in repo).

title: Hardy field world: ES for n = n(t) a function of a real parameter with eventual positivity
connection: Generalizing Z[T]: n(t) in a Hardy field (e.g. exp-log functions), denominators integer-valued exp-log functions eventually positive. Mordell–Schinzel's obstruction might weaken when exponentials are allowed (power ladders live here).
why: Gives the natural home of 'growing families': identities in exp-log functions of an auxiliary parameter k that cover square classes would have to evade T1 via exponential growth.
first_step: Test whether T1 at odd squares still blocks exp-log identities: does an identity in (k, 2^k) evaluate to certificate lines at squares?

title: World of 'n with prescribed factorization of n + 3': p ≡ 2 mod 3 trivial, p + 3 structure controls the x = (p+3)/4 slice
connection: The slice x = (p+3)/4 leaves 3/(px) = 1/y + 1/z, solvable iff px has a divisor ≡ 2 (mod 3) (or similar). So ES on the e = 3 slice is a statement about the prime factors of (p + 3)/4 modulo 3. Similar for e = 7, 11, … (each slice a 'world').
why: Each slice world is a congruence-on-factors world (a Chebotarev statement for p + e); the union over e is ES. Studying slice-world failure densities gives the per-slice ticket probability.
first_step: Compute, for p < 10^6, the failure density of the e-slice for e = 3, 7, 11, 15, 19 and compare with independence predictions.

title: Square-class depth: number of moduli M ≤ X with p ≡ square mod M — a T1-depth invariant of p
connection: T1 says certificate lines are empty at squares; a prime p ≡ 1 (mod M) behaves like a square modulo M. The count D(p) = #{M ≤ X : p is a square mod M} (or the largest smooth M with p ≡ 1 mod M) measures how 'square-like' p is.
why: If #ES(p) anti-correlates with D(p), hard primes are 'locally square-like' — a precise version of the smooth-(p − 1) observation and a direct link between hardness and T1.
first_step: Compute D(p) for p < 2·10^4 and correlate with #ES(p) and with constrained-world failures.

title: Connection: Erdős's multiplication-table / divisor-in-interval as obstruction to ES Type II sizes
connection: Type II needs e | a+b with 4ab | p+e — divisibility plus size constraints; Ford's multiplication-table theory gives the density of integers with divisors in intervals, which bounds Type II counts.
why: Explains why counts are log-power and not power: integers with structured divisors are rare (Ford's (log)^{−0.086} factor).
first_step: Check Elsholtz–Tao's use of divisor-sum bounds and whether Ford-type exponents appear in ES lower-tail estimates.

title: Connection: ES with 'one denominator a prime power of p' only (x = p^k·u)
connection: Restricting which denominators carry p changes the family set (Type I vs II). Pure Type I or pure Type II counts are each ≍ log³-intensity in the residue model?
why: If one type alone has intensity growing fast enough, ES could in principle be proved within one type; the computation can split intensities by type.
first_step: Modify scripts/z52b_dividing_avoid.py to run Type I only and Type II only; fit exponents separately.

title: U(n) never equals 5 (n ≤ 30 000)
connection: The value 5 is the only k ≤ 500 not attained by U(n) for 2 ≤ n ≤ 30 000; at primes ≤ 2·10⁵ the values 5 and 12 are never attained.
why: A gap in the value set is a cheap arithmetic fingerprint; if U(n) ≥ 6 eventually were provable by a structural lower bound it would be a (weak) quantitative ES statement for large n — but likely just small-n accident.
first_step: Extend U(n) to n ≤ 10⁵ and check whether U(n) = 5 ever appears; list all n with U(n) ≤ 8 and test whether they are all ≤ some bound.

title: U(232 792 561) = 276: the lcm(1..19)+1 prime is hard but not extreme
connection: p = lcm(1,…,19)+1 has U = 276, U/log²p = 0.74, U/log³p = 0.039 vs median U/log³p ≈ 0.095 at 10⁷ (below the minimum of 113 random primes at 10⁷); k₁ = 193, k₂ = 83 (k₁/k₂ = 2.3, typical). [An earlier version reported k₁ = 47 < k₂ = 82 — an artefact of a 64-bit overflow in the type classification, fixed after review.]
why: Partially confirms the lcm+1 prediction (hard, ≈ 2.5× below typical) but not 'record-hard'; the Type I/II split is normal, so all-small-primes-split does not starve Type I specifically at this prime.
first_step: Model-guided search for primes ≡ 1 (mod 2520·11·13) ≤ 10¹⁰ with extreme L(1,χ_p); compare their U/log³p with the lcm(1..19)+1 value.
alt_first_steps: [fingerprint-0012] Run z52b_count on 232792561 (needs ~3 GB spf sieve; or patch to factor x by trial division) and check R(p) via the words sieve extended to 2.4·10⁸.

title: (7/p) anomaly: U(p) does not see the character at 7
connection: Residual Spearman of U(p) with (2/p), (3/p), (5/p) is −0.55, −0.31, −0.28 but with (7/p) only −0.013, although Mordell's classes p ≡ 3,5,6 (mod 7) are covered by identities.
why: Suggests the mod-7 identity contributes O(1) solutions while 2,3,5 contribute families ∝ log p; identifies which local primes matter for the count — relevant to any weighted covering.
first_step: Split U(p) by p mod 7 class and by whether the mod-7 identity solution exists; check whether the 7-family has bounded size.

title: Uv(p) (U-certificates) ~ U(p): ρ = +0.64; R(p) only +0.24
connection: The ES count U(p) correlates +0.64 with the U-certificate word count Uv(p), +0.46 with I3(p), +0.32 with W(p) but only +0.24 with the (★) count R(p).
why: R(p) is a thin slice with its own character (χ_{−4p}); Uv tracks the whole count. Useful when choosing which certificate family to attack for a lower bound proportional to U(p).
first_step: Compute what fraction of each p's ES solutions correspond to (★), U, I3 words via the explicit maps; check whether the fraction is stable.

title: Greedy-failure composites: 49, 169, 361, 553, … (squares and products)
connection: The composite members of the x=(n+3)/4 failure set include many odd squares ≡ 1 (24) (49, 169, 361, 961, 1369, …) but not all (25 is certified: 4/25 = 1/7 + 1/70 + 1/350 with 7 = (25+3)/4), and non-squares like 553 = 7·79, 721, 793, 889.
why: Squares are over-represented (a T1-like effect for a single identity family) but not uniformly obstructed; non-square composite failures show the obstruction is not only quadratic.
first_step: List non-square composite members ≤ 10⁵ and check whether each factors into primes that are themselves failures (multiplicativity test).

title: k₁(n), k₂(n) are new sequences
connection: Number of solutions of 4/n with exactly one (k₁) / two (k₂) denominators divisible by n: k₁ = 0,2,0,1,5,5,0,5,6,6,9,…; k₂ = 1,1,1,1,2,2,2,1,4,3,…; neither in OEIS.
why: At primes these are ET Type I/Type II counts; separate sequences make it possible for others to find formulas.
first_step: Submit both (with k₃ ≡ 0 for n>1, a trivial lemma) to OEIS after independent verification.

title: k₂(p) ≥ 1 for every prime p ≤ 2·10⁵
connection: Every prime ≤ 2·10⁵ has a solution with exactly two denominators divisible by p (Type II); min k₂(p) over p ≡ 1 (4) > 1000 is small but nonzero.
why: ET note Type II is the 'easier to count' type; empirical universality of Type II alone is the statement many campaign lines target.
first_step: Record the minimum k₂(p) per dyadic range and list primes with k₂(p) = 1.

title: k₁(p) can be small while k₂(p) is not — or vice versa?
connection: k₁ and k₂ have residual correlation driven by different characters; tabulating the joint distribution of (k₁(p), k₂(p)) shows whether simultaneous smallness is rarer than independence predicts.
why: Anti-correlation of the types' local obstructions would be the cleanest heuristic for 'one type always works'.
first_step: Compute Spearman(k₁ residual, k₂ residual) and the count of p with both below their 5% quantiles vs 0.25% expected.

title: U(p) at p ≡ 1 (24) vs p ≡ 1 (840) distributions
connection: Spearman of residual U(p) with 1[p≡1 mod 24] is −0.62, with '840-square class' −0.38, with 1[p≡1 mod 840] −0.15 (rare event).
why: Quantifies how much of hardness is the classical Mordell residue structure — a reference point for any proof that treats 'bad residue classes' separately.
first_step: Compute mean U(p)/log²p per class mod 840 (the six square classes 1,121,169,289,361,529) and rank them.

title: R-zeros and Type-A failures across numerators: 193 fails 19 numerators, 577 13, 2521 11, 3361 11, 409 7, 9601 5, 5569 4, 66529 3, 23929 0
connection: Among m ∈ [5,48], the campaign's hard primes fail many m/p; but 23929 (an R-zero) fails none — R-failure is not 'globally hard'.
why: Separates certificate-line hardness ((★) zeros) from intrinsic ES hardness — useful to decide which hard primes are artefacts of a chosen line.
first_step: For each of the 14 R-zeros compute U(p)/log²p and H(p) to rank 'intrinsic' vs 'line-specific' hardness.

title: Joint zeros of R and Uv among n ≡ 1 (4)
connection: Since R (t ∈ 4ℤ) and Uv (v ∈ 𝒞_n) are different slices of the same word equation, their joint zero set among n≡1(4) non-squares should be tiny.
why: A two-line union covering all primes is the most economical certificate statement; FRONTIER notes (★) ∪ b=1 never fails ≤ 10⁸.
first_step: Compute the joint zero set of (R, Uv) and of (R, I3) ≤ 3·10⁶ from words_3e6.npy.

title: R(p) correlates with τ(4p+1)? — divisor-form check
connection: R(p) = Σ_C #{d | 4Cp+1 : d ≡ −1 (mod 4C)}; the C=1 term is #{d | 4p+1 : d ≡ 3 (mod 4)}; minz(p)/p correlates −0.42 with τ(4p+1).
why: Quantifies how much of R comes from C = 1 — if most, the (★) problem is essentially about one integer 4p+1 (a 'single shifted prime' divisor problem).
first_step: Compute the C-profile of R(p): fraction of R from C = 1, 2, 3, … at p ≤ 10⁶.

title: k₂ (Type II) is more sensitive to 3 than k₁: ρ((3/p)) = −0.41 vs −0.25
connection: Residual k₂(p) correlates −0.41 with (3/p) and −0.39 with v₃(p−1); k₁(p) correlates −0.25 and −0.25.
why: Type II solutions come from divisors of p-tied integers in classes mod 4C; C = 3 multiples are cheap — p ≡ 2 (mod 3) helps Type II most.
first_step: Count Type II solutions by C (the c=1 parameter) and check which C carry the 3-dependence.

title: k₁ (Type I) is more sensitive to 5 than k₂: ρ((5/p)) = −0.32 for k₁
connection: Residual k₁ correlates −0.32 with (5/p); k₂ less (not in top list).
why: Different local primes drive the two types; designing a covering argument per type should exploit their complementary local profiles.
first_step: Build a table ρ(type, (q/p)) for q ≤ 50 and both types.

title: k₂ correlates with spf(p+4) (−0.35)
connection: Smallest prime factor of p+4 anticorrelates with k₂(p): p+4 with small factors → more Type II solutions.
why: p+4 = 4·((p+3)/4)+1… p+4 divisors are the b=1, d=1 line; small factors give many small divisors in classes ≡ −1 (mod 4C).
first_step: Check ρ(k₂, spf(p+4C)) for C = 1..10.

title: ρ(U, I3(p)) = +0.46, ρ(U, W(p)) = +0.32
connection: Word counts at the same prime predict the ES count moderately; I3 more than all words.
why: I3 words (t,u,v ≥ 3) are a 'bulk' certificate family; strong correlation means I3 sees most of the arithmetic driving U.
first_step: Check whether I3(p) also follows χ_p (it does weakly: α ≈ −0.12) and whether its residual is mostly noise.

title: Mordell's identity classes as indicator features: which one explains most variance?
connection: For each classical polynomial identity (mod 3, 5, 7, 8, 11, …) define 1[p in identity class] and regress U(p) on all of them.
why: Identifies the identities that matter for the *count*, not just existence — a 'weighting' of the Mordell covering useful for heuristics.
first_step: Encode Mordell's and Vaughan's identity classes (cf. MODEL_SPECIFIC.md) as features and run a LASSO.

title: (★) count R(p): weights β₃ = −0.15, β₇ = −0.08, β₅ = +0.03 (p ≡ 1 mod 4)
connection: R(p)'s per-prime profile differs from U's: dominated by 3 and 7 (both ≡ 3 mod 4) with 5, 17 slightly positive — i.e. R follows (−1/q)(q/p) = χ_{−4p}(q) at q ≡ 1 (4) partially.
why: Pinpoints which local primes the (★) line is sensitive to — a covering argument for (★) should treat 3 and 7 specially.
first_step: Compute the 3-adic and 7-adic local densities of (★) triples (u,B,C) as a function of p mod 3, mod 7.

title: I3 count has β₇ = +0.039 (p ≡ 1 mod 4): QR at 7 helps I3
connection: Unlike U, I3(p) gains when 7 is a QR mod p; k₂ and Uv have β₇ ≈ −0.045.
why: Different certificate families have opposite responses at the same local prime — evidence for complementary families (union arguments) at the level of local densities.
first_step: Tabulate sign(β_q) per family for q ≤ 50 and find pairs of families with opposite sign at many q.

title: Least C with a (★) certificate vs p mod small numbers
connection: Cmin(p) (least C with a divisor d | 4Cp+1, d ≡ −1 (4C)) should depend on p mod 3, 5, 7 via which C make 4Cp+1 divisible by small primes.
why: A table of E[Cmin | p mod 840] is a direct, computable covering-cost fingerprint.
first_step: Compute Cmin for p ≤ 10⁶ and average by p mod 840.

title: Carmichael numbers are ES-rich, not ES-hard: U(n) is 3.3–5.7× the neighbour median
why: Although n ≡ 1 modulo each p−1 (the 'hard' congruence shape), having ≥ 3 prime factors multiplies divisor structure; the p ≡ 1 (mod L) hardness mechanism does not survive multiplicatively — hardness is a prime phenomenon.
first_step: Compare with semiprimes pq where both p, q are ES-hard (e.g. 193·241) to see whether hardness compounds at all.

title: Pairwise union conjecture: (★) ∪ U covers every non-square n ≡ 1 (4) ≤ 3·10⁶ except 105
connection: Joint zeros of R and Uv among non-square n ≡ 1 (mod 4), n ≤ 3·10⁶: only {105}. Same for R ∩ I3 = {105} and Uv ∩ I3 = {105}.
why: Any two of the three word families jointly certify ES on all non-square n ≡ 1 (4) in range (squares are T1-dead for all lines). A two-family statement is the most economical union target and stronger than FRONTIER's (★) ∪ b=1 at primes.
first_step: Extend the joint census to 10⁹ with the segmented sieve; try to find the local reason the families' failure sets are disjoint (different shift/character profiles, cf. per-prime weights).

title: (★) certificate size Cmin: records 1,2,5,20,23,39,40,141,149,251,557 then 23105 at p = 184837
connection: Least C with a (★) word at primes p ≡ 1 (4) ≤ 3·10⁶: mean 1.94, 99% quantile 9, 99.9% 41; the record jump to 23105 at 184837 is a boundary solution (u = 1, B = 2: 4C−1 = (p+1)/2), i.e. 184837 is an 'almost R-zero'.
why: Boundary-only primes (only u=1 or B=1 certificates) behave like R-zeros for any argument that excludes boundary terms; they enlarge the hard set for interior-only methods.
first_step: List all primes ≤ 3·10⁶ whose (★) words are boundary-only; compare their arithmetic profile with the R-zeros.

title: Boundary-only (★) primes as a second hardness list
connection: Compute-and-check: primes p ≡ 1 (4) where every (★) triple has u = 1 or B = 1 (trivial divisor of 4Cp+1 near the boundary); expect them to contain 184837 and be ~10× more numerous than R-zeros.
why: FRONTIER counts R(p) including boundary; interior counts are what equidistribution arguments control — so the interior-zero list is the real target of such arguments.
first_step: Modify the word sieve to count interior (★) words (u, B ≥ 2) and list zeros at primes ≤ 3·10⁶.

title: I3 needs large coordinates: min over I3 words of max(t,u,v) has median 169 and grows (740 at 2.5·10⁶)
connection: At primes p ≡ 1 (4) ≤ 3·10⁶ the smallest I3 certificate has max coordinate ≈ 175 on average, records 379 (487 381) … 740 (2 506 373).
why: I3 is cheap in count but expensive in size — unlike U and (★) (bounded small certificates); an existence proof for I3 can't use small-coordinate coverings.
first_step: Fit the record growth (≈ p^{0.3}?) and relate to the t,u,v ≥ 3 constraint geometry.

title: Mean (★) certificate size ≈ 2 and U size ≈ 4: most primes are certified by C ∈ {1,2}
connection: Cmin(p) = 1 for 76.6% of primes ≡ 1 (4) with a certificate and ≤ 2 for 91.8% (reviewer rerun): i.e. 4p+1 has a divisor ≡ −1 (mod 4), or 8p+1 one ≡ −1 (mod 8), for ≈ 92% of primes.
why: The (★) problem is mostly 'one or two shifted integers have a divisor in a class' — quantitative law: P(Cmin > c) decays fast; the tail (c ≥ 10) contains all hardness.
first_step: Fit P(Cmin > c) for c ≤ 50 and compare with the product of single-event failure probabilities ∏_{C≤c} P(4Cp+1 has no divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C).

title: Coprime-pair solutions fail at 1 285 primes (13, 37, 61, 97, 109, 181, 193, …)
connection: Solutions with gcd(x,y) = 1 (equivalently some coprime pair, identical failure set) are absent at 1 285 primes ≤ 10⁵, all apparently ≡ 1 (mod 12).
why: Pairwise-coprime structure fails generically on p ≡ 1 (12): every ES solution there shares factors — consistent with the 'multiplicative' Type I/II constructions.
first_step: Verify the mod-12 claim and compute the failure density in p ≡ 1 (12).

title: Primitive-failure primes vs R-zeros and Type-A failures
connection: 193 is a primitive failure; check overlap of the 110 primitive failures with the hard lists (R-zeros 409, 577, 5569, 9601, 23929, 83449 are p ≡ 1 (24); some are ≡ 1 (12)).
why: If primitive failures and line failures overlap strongly, the lines are 'primitive-solution detectors'.
first_step: Intersect the sets (variants.json) and compute the hypergeometric p-value.

title: BM residual correlation with U persists at 20 000–30 000: +0.58
connection: Residual Spearman(M_BM, U) = 0.65 (≤ 12 000) and 0.58 (20 000–30 000); with R only 0.10 / 0.10.
why: Robust: the campaign's BM main term is a strong predictor of the *total* ES count but not of its own (★) count fluctuations — suggests reorganising the BM analysis around U(p) or ESC(p).
first_step: Recompute the BM-type main term for the ESC family (all coordinates) and check whether it predicts ESC(p) fluctuations.

title: Autocorrelation of residual log U(n): lag 840 → 0.60, lag 120 → 0.49, lag 1 → −0.28
connection: The ES count sequence is strongly periodic with period 840 and anti-correlated at lag 1 (consecutive integers have opposite parity / mod-4 behaviour).
why: Ramanujan-expansion structure: U(n) ≈ Σ_q a_q c_q(n) with significant a_q for q | 840 — a clean target for a 'singular series' heuristic for the count over all n (not only primes).
first_step: Fit U(n)/log³n by Ramanujan sums c_q(n), q ≤ 120, and report the top coefficients (are they multiplicative in q?).

title: Class ordering within Mordell classes vs 3-adic depth
connection: 1 (mod 840) is hardest, 289 (mod 840) least among the six; p ≡ 1 (mod 9) vs 4,7 (mod 9) inside each class should explain part of it (9 vs 3 depth effect −0.03 measured earlier).
why: Gives the 'next layer' of Mordell's analysis: which further congruence (mod 9, 16, 25, 49, 11, 13) splits each hard class most.
first_step: Within p ≡ 1 (mod 840) primes, compute mean residual by p mod 9·16·25·11·13 factors one at a time.

title: Easiest classes mod 840: 557, 277, 653, 53, 317
connection: These classes have the most ES solutions on average (+0.3 to +0.54 in log); they are non-squares modulo several of 3, 5, 8 at once (e.g. 557 ≡ 2 mod 3, 2 mod 5, 5 mod 8).
why: The easy classes are covered by several identities simultaneously; counting how many Mordell identities cover each class and correlating with the class mean tests 'count ≈ number of covering identities'.
first_step: Enumerate Mordell/ET identity families mod 840 and count multiplicities per class; correlate with class means.

title: Census design: compute U only at model-predicted hard primes
connection: Since n mod 840 explains 64% and the χ_p Euler product most of the rest, a census of the hardest primes can target ≈ 1% of primes (p ≡ 1, 121, 361, 169, 529, 289 mod 840 with many small QRs).
why: Turns the global lower-envelope question into a feasible computation up to 10¹² for the candidate set.
first_step: Implement the pre-filter (840-class + q ≤ 23 QR count ≥ 6) and run the count on survivors in [10⁹, 10⁹ + 10⁷].

title: A396825/A397366 (van Tol): integers not in the 'S(n)' triangle — 12, 28, 33, 60, 96, 124, 193, 228, 288, 336, 385, …
connection: van Tol's S(n) = {A ≤ 4n−2 : A·X + W ≡ 0 (mod 4n−1) for divisors X, W of n}; complement A396825 contains all squares, all ≡ 0,1,4,9 (mod 12), and includes 193 (a Type-A failure) and 288, 336 (A287116), 12, 28, 60, 96, 124, 228 (our U-zero set Uv = 0).
why: Another divisor-class formulation whose exceptional set overlaps ours: aligning the three (A396825, A287116, our Uv/ESC zero sets) could reveal they are the same obstruction at different normalisations.
first_step: Compute the symmetric differences between A396825 ∩ [1, 3000] and our Uv/ESC/R zero sets; explain 33 and 193.

title: A400619's record prime 8 803 369 is ES-hard (U/log³p = 0.034) but not a (★) zero (R = 16)
connection: U(8803369) = 140 (k₁ = 94, k₂ = 46; overflow-corrected), U/log³p = 0.034 — below the 10⁶/10⁷ window minima 0.044/0.055 and below lcm(1..19)+1 (0.039); words: W = 107, I3 = 68, R = 16, Uv = 11. The nearby R-zero 8 813 281 has W = 127, R = 0.
why: Greedy-depth records are genuinely hard for the full count, while (★) zeros are line-specific: two independent hardness notions pick different primes at the same height.
first_step: Compute the χ_p Euler product and p mod 840 for 8803369 and 8813281; predict which notion each satisfies.

title: Our ESC zero set ≤ 1369 ⊂ A396825 ∪ {105, 672}
connection: Every n ≤ 1369 with no word having a coordinate in 4ℤ ∪ (8ℤ − n) is in van Tol's A396825 except 105 and 672; Uv zeros differ from A396825 by {33, 193, 385} vs {105, 156, 204, 316, 396, 508, …}.
why: Near-containment between independently defined exception sets suggests a common divisor-class obstruction; making it exact would merge two literatures.
first_step: Fetch the A396825 b-file and test containment to 10⁶; analyse 105 and 672 under van Tol's S(n) definition.

title: Per-class identity 'signatures' mod 840
connection: For each class a mod 840, the set of limiting ratios (y/x, z/x) of solutions common to all primes in the class is its identity signature; hard classes should have empty signatures (no polynomial identity).
why: Makes Mordell–Schinzel's 'no polynomial identity covers square classes' visible in data, and might expose quasi-identities (identities valid for a positive proportion of the class).
first_step: Group solutions by class and ratio buckets; list buckets present for ≥ 90% of primes in the class.

title: Quasi-identities: ratio buckets present for a positive proportion of a hard class
connection: In the six hard classes, find solution families (ratio buckets) present for ≥ 30% of primes; each corresponds to a conditional identity (valid when some auxiliary divisibility holds).
why: Conditional identities with complementary conditions could jointly cover a hard class — a 'covering by conditional identities' strategy whose obstacles the data would show.
first_step: Mine the solution lists of primes ≡ 1 (mod 840) ≤ 2·10⁵ for frequent ratio buckets and their auxiliary conditions.

title: ES count of the Fermat quotient-free / 'ES-easy' family p ≡ −1 (mod 840): exact identities
connection: Record-easy primes are ≡ −1 (mod 840); since p ≡ 3 (4) is trivially ES-solvable, the count excess there measures how many extra identity families fire at −1 modulo 3, 5, 7, 8.
why: The easy-side structure (all identities fire) quantifies the 'maximum covering multiplicity' — the dual of the hard side.
first_step: Mean U(p)/log³p over p ≡ 839 (mod 840) vs other p ≡ 3 (4).

title: Lag-840 correlation at primes: residual log U(p) vs U(p+840) = 0.64 (3 425 pairs); lag 5880: 0.58
connection: Among primes p ≡ 1 (4) with p + 840 also prime, residuals correlate 0.64 — the mod-840 class carries ≈ 60% of the variance at primes too.
why: Confirms at primes what the all-n spectrum showed: ES counts are dominated by a mod-840 periodic component plus a character (q ∤ 840) component.
first_step: Decompose the remaining 40% by p mod 11, 13 and by the χ_p Euler product over q ≥ 11.

title: Easy class −1 (mod 840): mean U/log³p = 0.70 vs 0.19 for other p ≡ 3 (4)
connection: Primes p ≡ 839 (mod 840) have 3.6× more ES solutions than other primes ≡ 3 (mod 4) (p > 1000).
why: Quantifies the covering multiplicity at the 'all identities fire' class — the dual extreme to p ≡ 1 (mod 840).
first_step: Count which classical identities apply at p ≡ −1 (mod 840) and check that their solution counts sum to the observed excess.

title: Degenerate-locus obstruction as a model for T1
connection: The isosceles locus of 4/p is obstructed exactly on p ≡ 1 (4) by a mod-4 factor-class argument on 2p²; T1 (all certificate lines empty at odd squares) is a reciprocity obstruction on p-tied integers.
why: Both are 'a fixed integer built from p has no divisor in a required class' — the isosceles case is the 0-dimensional toy model of the line obstructions, fully understood; studying how the obstruction disappears when one moves off the degenerate locus could illuminate why lines fail only at squares.
first_step: Parametrise near-isosceles solutions (y − x small) and compute when their divisor-class condition becomes solvable for p ≡ 1 (4).

title: Residual factor pairs
connection: Fixing x turns 4/p−1/x=a/b into (ay−b)(az−b)=b²; connect ES to complementary divisors in simultaneous residue classes.
why: This is an exact two-unit-fraction reformulation rather than a counting analogy.
first_step: For primes below 500, enumerate x up to p and record the successful residue pairs.

title: Resultants between identities
connection: Eliminate shared parameters from two valid ES families to identify their intersections and potential transition rules.
why: Intersections may show how families cooperate rather than merely duplicate coverage.
first_step: Compute a resultant for two small exact families found by direct denominator ansatz.

title: Voronoi-style dualization
connection: Check whether divisor-weighted progressions in an ES count fit a summation formula that exchanges long and short ranges.
why: A dual expression could reveal cancellation or a useful geometric interpretation.
first_step: Write the smoothed divisor sum explicitly and check available Voronoi formulas against its modulus dependence.

title: Shifted convolution of auxiliary integers
connection: Compare divisor counts of 4Cp+1 and 4Dp+1 as a shifted or linearly related convolution.
why: These correlations describe redundancy between certificate lines more precisely than independence heuristics.
first_step: Expand the mixed divisor count for C=1,D=2 and identify the underlying linear relation.

title: Divisor collision counting
connection: Count pairs of auxiliary values sharing a useful divisor and interpret the resulting linear relation between their parameters.
why: Collisions can create transfer rules between searches rather than merely redundant counts.
first_step: Solve d dividing both 4Cp+1 and 4Dp+1 and classify the resulting restrictions on C−D.

title: Digit lifting of identities
connection: Try extending a certificate for a truncated base expansion of p when one more digit is appended.
why: This is an induction proposal with exact algebraic correction terms, not an assumption that prime prefixes behave well.
first_step: Substitute p′=bp+r and x′=bx+a into the cleared equation and solve the first correction constraints.

title: Cluster expansions for factor dependence
connection: Group interacting prime-factor selections into connected clusters instead of treating them as independent residue choices.
why: A convergent or finite exact expansion could organize corrections to naive randomness.
first_step: For an auxiliary integer with at most six distinct factors, calculate connected correlation terms explicitly.

title: Tensor rank of identity families
connection: Represent coefficients of a bounded-degree ES ansatz as a tensor and seek low-rank structure.
why: Low-rank decompositions can propose separable parameter substitutions that are then checked symbolically.
first_step: Form the coefficient tensor of one cleared ansatz and inspect rank-one or rank-two decompositions over the rationals.

title: Optimal transport of divisor-residue measures
connection: Compare residue distributions from two auxiliary parameters using a cost based on allowed residue moves.
why: A low-cost transport plan might identify concrete transformations connecting complementary families.
first_step: For a small modulus, solve a finite transport problem between two divisor-residue histograms and inspect its dominant edges.

title: Counterexample-guided identity synthesis
connection: Alternate proposing symbolic denominator formulas with finding primes or parameter values violating their claimed domain.
why: Counterexamples refine the synthesis grammar while every accepted identity requires symbolic verification.
first_step: Run a small CEGIS loop over affine numerator and denominator templates restricted to one residue class.

title: Discrete-log coordinates with multiplicity constraints
connection: Use discrete logs only to linearize residues, retaining the bounded exponent ranges of actual divisors.
why: Solving the unrestricted linear congruence alone would create nonexistent divisors; bounded coefficients are essential.
first_step: Compare bounded and unrestricted exponent solutions in a small cyclic unit group and quantify spurious solutions.

title: Explaining count outliers
connection: For primes with unexpectedly few witnesses, decompose the prediction error into factorization, local-density, and family-overlap features.
why: An explanation may suggest a targeted new identity instead of merely another statistical model.
first_step: Select ten low-count outliers and compare each feature against matched primes of similar size.

title: Nonnegative latent mechanisms
connection: Factor a nonnegative count matrix into a few latent family and prime components, then seek arithmetic interpretations.
why: Unlike a proof, the factorization only suggests which mechanisms might be shared.
first_step: Fit ranks two through five and inspect whether components align with known gcd or character labels.

title: A dictionary of incompatible conventions
connection: Translate denominator ordering, primitive conditions, and sign conventions across candidate papers before comparing results.
why: Apparent contradictions or missed equivalences can come from different definitions.
first_step: Build a one-page convention table for three verified sources once located, including exact theorem hypotheses.

title: Parametric proof objects
connection: Represent an infinite family by a polynomial identity proof plus a separate modular integrality proof.
why: This makes the difference between many tested examples and a genuine family theorem explicit.
first_step: Define a record containing symbolic denominators, domain hypotheses, the identity, and integrality certificates.

title: Infinitesimal deformations and exact correction
connection: Compute tangent directions at a certificate, then ask which directions extend to rational curves with controllable denominators.
why: Tangent data can propose families, but exact substitution is required beyond first order.
first_step: Linearize the cleared equation at one small triple and test two tangent directions with quadratic correction terms.

title: KAM-type persistence: solutions of 4/n persist under small perturbation of n
connection: A solution for n yields solutions for multiples of n; conversely, do solutions 'persist' from n to n+1, n+2 via small rational moves (the way KAM tori persist)? ES across consecutive integers is a 'persistence' problem.
why: Elsholtz–Tao's identities for n ≡ 2,3 mod 4 are such persistence rules; a complete persistence rule along primes ≡ 1 mod 24 would be a proof; partial rules give covering systems (B1 — but we are breadth-first).
first_step: Compute, for consecutive primes p < q ≤ 10⁵, the minimal 'edit distance' between solution sets (e.g. number of solutions for q within Hamming distance 1 in (x,y,z)/scaled coordinates); look for structure.

title: Ehrenfest-style 'recurrence': ES solutions along the sequence p → p+24k as a Poincaré recurrence
connection: Fix a solution template (c,d,f) and ask for which k it still works for p+24k; the recurrence set is an AP-union (polynomial identity) or empty. The density of 'recurrence times' is a dynamical invariant.
why: Quantifies how much of ES is 'covered by local identities' vs genuinely new at each prime.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁴ and each solution, compute the set of k ≤ 10³ for which the same (c,d) with the forced f works for p+24k; histogram.

title: Statistical mechanics of covering systems: 'temperature' at which Mordell-style covers fail
connection: Each polynomial identity covers an AP of primes; covering systems have a Hough-type threshold (minimum modulus bounded). Translate: a complete ES cover by identities with moduli ≤ M is impossible (Mordell–Schinzel), but a cover with density 1 − δ(M) is possible; δ(M) is a 'free energy'.
why: The rate δ(M) → 0 quantifies B1 precisely; a slow decay says identities are not the way, a fast decay says the residual set is tiny and maybe handleable differently.
first_step: Compute δ(M) = density of residues mod M not covered by identities of degree ≤ 2 with parameter modulus ≤ M, for M = 840, 1680, 2520, …; fit.
refs: Hough, 'Solution of the minimum modulus problem for covering systems'

title: Fisher-information / Cramér–Rao bound on how well p mod M predicts f(p)
connection: Treat f(p) as a signal and residues of p mod various M as features; the mutual information I(f(p); p mod M) measures how much of ES is 'local'. Mordell's classes are the M=840 case.
why: A rigorous statement 'f(p) is asymptotically independent of p mod M for all M' would be a theorem of equidistribution type; conversely strong dependence would point to new identities.
first_step: Compute I(f(p) ≥ k; p mod M) for M | 2⁵·3²·5·7·11·13 and p ≤ 10⁷; list the M with highest information per bit.

title: Factoring with hints (Rivest–Shamir, Maurer): ES as 'one divisor with 1/2 of the bits known'
connection: If a divisor f of 4Cp+1 is ≡ −1 mod 4C, then its low bits (mod 4C) are known; Maurer/Rivest–Shamir show factoring with half the bits known is polynomial. Conversely the *existence* of such a 'half-known' divisor for some C is ES.
why: The crypto literature's reverse question — for which N do such hint-structured divisors exist for a given hint modulus — may have been studied for key-generation (e.g. 'RSA keys with prescribed residue primes').
first_step: Search 'divisors in a prescribed residue class existence density Lenstra' (Lenstra 1984, 'Divisors in residue classes'): Lenstra bounds the NUMBER of divisors in a class by a constant when M > N^{1/3}; check what this says about ES's counting shape (at most O(1) certificates per large C).
refs: H. W. Lenstra Jr., 'Divisors in residue classes', Math. Comp. 42 (1984)

title: Approximate-GCD problem (van Dijk–Gentry–Halevi–Vaikuntanathan) and the Type I form
connection: Type I: f | p² + 4c²d with f ≡ −p mod 4cd. Many samples p² + 4c²d (varying c,d) each near a multiple of an unknown f is the 'approximate GCD' setting from homomorphic encryption; its hardness/easiness results describe when such common divisors exist.
why: AGCD theory has precise density statements for when noisy multiples share a divisor; flipping to existence is an ES-like 'tied' question.
first_step: Write the Type I condition as p² ≡ −4c²d (mod f): a quadratic residuosity condition (−d is a square mod f up to units). Compare with the AGCD lattice attack (Cohn–Heninger 2011) to see whether it enumerates ES certificates.

title: Gröbner basis / elimination for the system {Type I condition, Type II condition} as polynomial equations with p symbolic
connection: The Type I/II parametrisations are polynomial identities in (c,d,f,p). Elimination ideals over ℤ[p] could expose hidden relations between simultaneous Type I and Type II solutions of the same p.
why: Relations between the two types (e.g. a Type I solution implies a Type II for a related prime) would be a new 'persistence' tool.
first_step: In Singular/Macaulay2, set up the ideal generated by 4xyz − p(xy+yz+zx) with x = pA, etc., and compute elimination ideals; look for any surprise generator.

title: Pseudo-Boolean / ILP relaxation: lower bound f(p) via LP duality on the e-slice counting polytope
connection: Write f(p) = Σ over e-slices of #{(a,b)}; an LP relaxation with constraints from divisor-sum identities (Σ_e over slices of total divisor counts = known) might give a dual certificate f(p) ≥ 1 if the identities are strong enough.
why: LP duality turns 'existence' into 'an explicit positive combination of known identities exceeds 0' — a proof template that is mechanically checkable.
first_step: Set up for p = 1009 (small): variables = indicator of each (e, a, b) candidate; constraints = all linear identities the campaign knows (divisor totals per e, M_BM-type sums); solve the LP; see whether the LP bound is > 0.

title: Is C_min(p) actually bounded? (sanity question separating covering from identities)
connection: Mordell–Schinzel forbids *polynomial* identities on square classes but does not forbid 'for every prime p ≡ 1 mod 24 some C ≤ 10⁶ works'. If C_min is empirically bounded (e.g. ≤ 1000 up to 10¹⁸) that is a striking structural fact; if it grows like log p, there is no finite cover at all.
why: This is the single most basic calibration of the 'covering' approach and the question is sharp and cheap.
first_step: git grep -il 'C_min\|bounded C\|smallest C' -- '*.md'; if absent, compute max_{p ≤ 10⁸} C_min(p) with C in Type II form and in e-slice form.

title: Yamamoto's 1965 proof that odd squares have no Type I/II solutions — read the original for *spare* structure
connection: Yamamoto's argument (reciprocity) is T1. Original papers often contain more than the cited theorem (e.g. a characterisation of which n have f_I = 0).
why: If Yamamoto characterised all n with f_I(n) = 0 (not just squares) the campaign's U(n) sporadics {105, 2961, …} might be explained; also his method's 'failure at squares' may be invertible into a 'success at non-squares' condition.
first_step: Obtain Yamamoto, 'On the Diophantine equation 4/n = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z', Mem. Fac. Sci. Kyushu Univ. 19 (1965); read all lemmas; compare with the U(n) sporadic list.

title: Gauss composition / Bhargava cubes for the Type II identity ff′ − 4c²dp = 1
connection: ff′ − (2c)²dp = 1 is a 'norm form equals 1' type equation: ff′ − D·1 = 1 with D = 4c²dp; i.e. the matrix [[f, 2c√d],[2c√d·p... ]] — more precisely it says f·f′ ≡ 1 mod 4c²dp. Bhargava's parametrisation of ideal classes by 2×2×2 cubes might organise the triples (f, f′, 4c²d) with product structure.
why: Composition laws give group structure on solution sets of quadratic-type equations; a group structure on ES certificates for fixed p would be a huge structural input (cf. Markoff).
first_step: Check whether the set of Type II certificates for fixed p carries a natural binary operation (e.g. via the ideal (f, p + 2c√−d) composition); test on p = 1009: list certificates and look for closure.

title: Choose C = (p−1)/4 or C = (p+3)/4 etc.: 'self-referential' C that make 4Cp+1 factor algebraically
connection: If C is a polynomial in p, 4Cp + 1 is a polynomial in p which may factor: e.g. C = p gives 4p² + 1 (irreducible); C = (p² − 1)/4 ... gives p³ − p + 1; C = 2p+1... Algebraic factorisations give guaranteed divisors; the residue condition then is a polynomial congruence — i.e. this IS the polynomial-identity route (B1), but with quadratic/cubic C. Mordell–Schinzel covers all polynomial C? It covers polynomial x,y,z; polynomial C ⟹ polynomial (x,y,z). So yes.
why: Still worth listing: identities with C = polynomial of degree ≥ 3 are not in Mordell's table, and the theorem forbids them only on square classes — maybe they cover *more* of the non-square classes (reducing the residual set to exactly the squares mod a larger modulus?).
first_step: Enumerate C = aP(p) for small polynomials P of degree ≤ 3, factor 4Cp+1 symbolically, check which residue classes mod 840·k get covered.

title: p-adic Hensel-lifting view: ES at p is a statement about the p-adic unit 4/p... no — about x,y,z with exactly one or two divisible by p (Type I/II)
connection: Type I: p | x only; write x = pX. Then 4/p = 1/(pX) + 1/y + 1/z ⟹ (4X − 1)/(pX) = 1/y + 1/z. So Type I ⟺ (4X−1)/(pX) is a two-term Egyptian fraction for some X. Type II: x = pX, y = pY: 4/p − 1/(pX) − 1/(pY) = (4XY − X − Y)/(pXY) = 1/z ⟹ z = pXY/(4XY − X − Y): Type II ⟺ (4XY − X − Y) | pXY. Since gcd(4XY−X−Y, XY) | ... these are the 'words' p = tuv − u − v? Let me not resolve; the item: make the X-parametrisations the primary object and study the p-adic valuations.
why: Explicit small-parameter forms (X, Y) make 'Type II ⟺ ∃ X,Y: (4XY − X − Y) | pXY' which with gcd analysis becomes 4XY − X − Y = p·(divisor of XY)/... The repo's word form p = tuv − u − v is this. Keep as the 'word' entry point for the free lane.
first_step: Derive carefully: Type II ⟺ ∃ X, Y ≥ 1 with (4XY − X − Y) | pXY; show this is equivalent to p = tuv − u − v with 4 | t (repo's statement) and record the dictionary.
refs: FRONTIER.md §1 words p = tuv − u − v

title: The word form p = tuv − u − v with t ∈ 4ℤ: 'every prime is tuv − u − v with 4 | t' as a multiplicative-additive representation problem
connection: p + u + v = tuv with t = 4C ⟺ 4Cp + 1 = (4Cu − 1)(4Cv − 1): so 'some 4Cp+1 factors as a product of two numbers ≡ −1 mod 4C' is a SUFFICIENT condition for ES (it is the c = 1 sub-case of Type II; it gives x = Cuv, y = pCv, z = pCu). Full Type II is ff′ = 4c²dp + 1 with the weaker congruence f ≡ f′ ≡ −1 (mod 4cd). Sanity computation (scripts/z52b_free_fable_sanity.py): the C-form is strictly weaker — p = 409, 577, 5569, 9601 have no C-form certificate with C < 1500 although they have Type II certificates (409: c=2, d=1, f=7, f′=935).
why: The C-form is the cleanest 'tied-modulus' statement (N = 4Cp+1, modulus 4C | N − 1) and covers all but a thin set of primes; the exceptions are themselves a lead (what distinguishes 409, 577, 5569, 9601?). 5569 ≡ 529 and 9601 ≡ 361 (mod 840) are Mordell-hard.
first_step: Extend the census: primes p ≤ 10⁶ with no C-form certificate for C ≤ 10⁴; density (→ 0? constant?); Legendre profiles of the exceptions; then the general question G(m,k): does mk+1 have a divisor ≡ −1 mod m.

title: C-form as an explicit infinite covering system of residue classes (and it provably does NOT cover all primes)
connection: Fix a ≡ −1 (mod 4C), a | 4Cp+1 ⟺ p ≡ −(4C)^{−1} (mod a). So the c = 1 Type II certificates form the explicit system of classes {−(4C)^{−1} mod a : C ≥ 1, a ≡ −1 mod 4C}; full Type II adds classes {−(4c²d)^{−1} mod a : a ≡ −1 mod 4cd}; Type I adds its own. ES ⟺ the union of these explicit infinite systems covers all primes ≡ 1 mod 24. The c = 1 subsystem alone misses 409, 577, 5569, 9601 (C < 1500 checked).
why: 'Does an explicit infinite set of congruence classes with unbounded moduli cover all primes' is a question with its own tools (Erdős covering theory, density of unions, sieve), and the T1 obstruction says the union misses all odd squares — so the full system is a covering of ℕ ∖ {odd squares} ∖ (sporadics?).
first_step: Compute the density of integers covered by the c=1 classes with a ≤ A as A grows (inclusion–exclusion); then add the (c,d) classes; identify uncovered integers ≤ 10⁶ and compare with odd squares + U(n) sporadics.

title: Odd squares m² are uncovered by the (C, a) covering system — turn this into a *characterisation* of uncovered integers
connection: T1 says no Type I/II solutions at odd squares; in the covering language, m² ≡ −(4C)^{−1} mod a with a ≡ −1 mod 4C never holds (reciprocity). Ask: are odd squares the ONLY uncovered integers (together with the U(n) sporadics 105, 2961, 3985, 25305, 111969, 978145 — which concern a related but different U(n) statement; check which)? If the uncovered set is exactly {odd squares} ∪ finite, then ES is 'covering system misses exactly the squares', a Rickards–Stange-type statement.
why: This is the cleanest 'squares + sporadic' statement; it's a conjecture, but the structure (reciprocity makes squares fail) suggests the mechanism to prove coverage of non-squares is a 'quadratic reciprocity + something' argument.
first_step: Compute the uncovered set for n ≤ 10⁶ (all n) under full Type II (all (c,d) with 4c²d ≤ bound) and separately under Type I; compare with odd squares and the U(n) sporadics; note the c=1 subsystem already misses 409, 577, 5569, 9601.

title: Closure of winning C under multiplication: if 4Cp+1 = ab with a,b ≡ −1 mod 4C, what about C' = Ck?
connection: 4Ckp + 1 — relation to ab: 4Ckp + 1 = k(ab − 1) + 1 = kab − k + 1. No obvious divisor. But via the (x,y,z) form: a solution for p from C gives (x,y,z); scaling doesn't change C. So no direct closure; but the e-slice form (e ≡ −p mod 4) might have closure: if e works, does e·k work? Check.
why: Any closure property on the certificate set would be a group-like structure (cf. Markoff orbits); worth 10 minutes of computation.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁴, list winning e-slices and winning C; test closure under multiplication by small k and under 'e ↦ 4N − e'-type involutions.

title: Involutions on the certificate set: swapping a ↔ b in 4Cp+1 = ab, and the (x,y,z) permutation symmetry
connection: Each Type II certificate (C, a, b) is unordered in {a,b}; each solution (x,y,z) has S₃ symmetry. Counting orbits rather than solutions might reveal parity structure (f(p) odd?) — Markoff's count mod p came from orbit sizes.
why: Involution-counting is the canonical 'rigidity' existence proof; even the failure analysis (no fixed points ⟹ even count ⟹ no info) is worth stating.
first_step: Define the full certificate set S_p = {(C, a, b)} for p ≤ 10⁴; compute |S_p| mod 2 (expect even) and look for another involution (e.g. (C, a, b) ↦ (C', a', b') via the Type I ↔ Type II relation) with a computable fixed-point set.

title: Analytic continuation trick: define F_p(s) = Σ_C C^{−s} · #{d | 4Cp+1, d ≡ −1 (4C)} and study its pole/residue at s = 1
connection: If F_p(s) has a simple pole at s = 1 with residue R(p) > 0 computable from local data, then infinitely many C win (for each p) — ES(p) with a vengeance. The residue would come from the 'main term' of the C-average, which the campaign computes as M_BM. The question is whether F_p(s) continues and whether the residue is provably positive — i.e., whether a *Tauberian* argument works at fixed p.
why: Tauberian arguments at fixed p would be a new shape: the Dirichlet series in C at fixed p is a 'vertical' object (like a Dirichlet series of a shifted-divisor problem Σ τ(4Cp+1)C^{−s}, which DOES continue meromorphically with a pole at s=1 — Estermann/Ingham-type). The residue-class restriction d ≡ −1 (4C) is the new feature.
first_step: Study the simpler series Σ_C τ(4Cp+1)C^{−s} (known: continuation via Estermann's treatment of Σ τ(an+b)n^{−s}); then insert the character condition and see if the continuation survives with an explicit residue.

title: ES for primes in a fixed Chebotarev class of a big compositum: a 'conditional on splitting' infinite family
connection: Fix the splitting of p in K = ℚ(i, √2, √3, √5, √7, …) (finitely many Legendre symbols); for a given profile, does a *fixed* Type I/II template (with d, c chosen by the profile) always work? That would be an identity depending on Legendre symbols — not polynomial, so not excluded by Mordell–Schinzel.
why: Legendre-symbol-dependent identities are a natural, unexplored (?) class strictly larger than polynomial identities. Even partial coverage (e.g. all profiles except those where p is a square mod all small primes — which includes squares!) would be a beautiful structural statement matching T1.
first_step: For primes ≤ 10⁷ with profile (p mod 840, (p/q) for q ≤ 31), check whether the first winning template (C, a mod 4C) is constant on the profile class; count profile classes with a constant template.

title: Does ES hold for the square-like composites m² + 24k with small k? (near-square test)
connection: Odd squares are the obstruction for Type I/II; integers *near* squares in the Legendre-profile sense (QR mod many primes) or in size (m² + small) are the natural 'almost obstruction' test; if f(m² + 24) is systematically small, the obstruction has a 'continuity' which a proof would need to respect.
why: Empirical probe of 'how localised' T1 is.
first_step: Compute f(n) for n = m² + 24k, k = 1..5, m ≤ 10⁴ (n not necessarily prime; use Type I/II counts); compare with random n of the same size.

title: Composite n and the 'certificate from a factor' loophole: ES(n) for n = pq follows from ES(p); but are there composites with NO Type I/II solution other than squares and the sporadics?
connection: The U(n) list (105, 2961, 3985, 25305, 111969, 978145) are exactly such sporadics (for the U(n) statement). Understanding WHY 105 = 3·5·7 fails the direct Type I/II test while 3, 5, 7 each succeed — a 'non-transfer' of certificates to products — is a small concrete structure question.
why: Sporadics are the fingerprints of the mechanism; their factorisations (105 = 3·5·7; 2961 = 3²·7·47; 3985 = 5·797; 25305 = 3·5·7·241; 111969 = 3·37·1009? check; 978145 = 5·...?) might share a pattern (many small primes ≡ 3 mod 4? products of a square and something?).
first_step: Factor all six sporadics; compute their Legendre profiles; list which small C fail and why (subgroup type or few factors); see if a common structural reason emerges.

title: Finding: the t ∈ 4ℤ word form (c = 1 Type II) misses primes 409, 577, 5569, 9601 — study the exceptions
connection: Sanity computation during this lane: among primes p ≡ 1 (mod 4) below 20000, exactly four (409, 577, 5569, 9601 — all ≡ 1 mod 24; 5569 ≡ 529 and 9601 ≡ 361 mod 840 are Mordell-hard) have no factorisation 4Cp + 1 = ab with a ≡ b ≡ −1 (mod 4C) for any C < 1500, while all have Type II certificates with c ≥ 2 (409: 16p+1 = 7·935, 7 ≡ 935 ≡ −1 mod 8). Extended search: none of the four has a C-form certificate with C ≤ 60000.
why: The c = 1 form is the one most 'tied-modulus' statements in this list implicitly use; knowing it is strictly weaker than ES, and which primes escape it, is a concrete structural datum. If the exceptions have infinite C_min in the c=1 form, then the c ≥ 2 congruence slack (mod 4cd instead of 4c²d) is *essential* — a fact a proof must use.
first_step: Prove a local obstruction for these p: every C-form divisor a satisfies (a/p) = −1 (see the next finding), so a C-form certificate needs a QNR divisor a ≡ −1 (mod 4C) of 4Cp+1; look for a further forced symbol (e.g. (2/p), (−1/p)_4, p mod 16: 577, 5569, 9601 ≡ 1 mod 16 but 409 ≡ 9) that makes this impossible; otherwise extend the search to C ≤ 10⁷ with Pari.

title: Finding/lemma: every C-form certificate divisor a of 4Cp+1 is a quadratic non-residue mod p ((a/p) = −1), and this reproves T1 for the C-form
connection: If a | 4Cp+1 with a ≡ −1 (mod 4C) then 4Cp ≡ −1 (mod a), so (4Cp/a) = (−1/a) = −1 (a ≡ 3 mod 4). Quadratic reciprocity gives (C/a) = +1 for a ≡ −1 (mod 4C) (odd part: (C′/a) = (a/C′)(−1)^{(C′−1)/2} = (−1/C′)(−1)^{(C′−1)/2} = 1; 2-part: a ≡ 7 mod 8 when 8 | a+1 so (2/a) = 1). Hence (p/a) = −1 and, as p ≡ 1 mod 4, (a/p) = −1. Verified for all 1798 certificates with p < 3000, C < 80. For p = m² this is impossible ((a/m²) = +1): T1 in two lines. The cofactor b = (4Cp+1)/a is also a QNR mod p (b ≡ a^{−1} mod p).
why: A necessary condition on certificates that is *not* a residue condition on C alone — it couples a with p. It halves the candidate divisors and suggests the exceptional primes (409, 577, 5569, 9601) may be explained by a further forced symbol. It also makes the C-form a purely 'QNR-divisor' problem: find C with a QNR (mod p) divisor a ≡ −1 (mod 4C) of 4Cp+1.
first_step: Do the same computation for full Type II (f ≡ f′ ≡ −1 mod 4cd, ff′ = 4c²dp+1): is (f/p) forced? (Expect (f/p) = (−d/·)-twisted.) Then for Type I. Then try to use the QNR condition positively: among divisors a ≡ −1 mod 4C of 4Cp+1, QR and QNR mod p should be equidistributed by a Pólya–Vinogradov-type argument over C — i.e. the condition costs a factor 1/2, no more.

title: Meta: maintain a single 'dictionary of forms' table (Type I, Type II, C-form, e-slice, word, ES₅, U_n, quaternion) with exact equivalence scopes
connection: This lane found that one popular form (C-form) is strictly weaker than Type II; the repo has ≥ 8 reformulations and their mutual implications are scattered. A one-page table 'form A ⟹ form B (scope, proof pointer, counterexample if not ⟺)' prevents wasted lanes.
why: Cheap, high-leverage: half the items in any breadth lane depend on which form they silently assume.
first_step: Create REFORMULATIONS.md with a matrix of implications among the 8 forms, each entry with a pointer or a small counterexample (e.g. 409 for C-form vs Type II).

title: Meta: adopt 'squares + sporadic' as the official conjecture shape for Type II alone and for Type I alone
connection: Instead of ES itself, state: 'f_II(n) = 0 iff n is an odd square or n ∈ S_II (finite)'; similarly Type I. These are stronger, type-separated conjectures with their own sporadic lists, cheaper to test, and their mechanism (reciprocity obstruction only at squares) is more precisely what HKRS/RS handle.
why: Separating types might reveal that one type has a *provable* 'squares + sporadic' structure (e.g. Type I via class-group/ternary-form theory, Duke–Schulze-Pillot style) even if the other doesn't.
first_step: Compute S_I and S_II (n ≤ 10⁷, all n) and see if they stabilise; then check Type I's structure against representation-by-ternary-forms theorems.

title: Erdős covering-system theory: the C-form classes have moduli a ≡ −1 (mod 4C) for each C — density of the union by Erdős–Selfridge-style inclusion–exclusion
connection: The union over C and a ≡ −1 (4C) of the classes r_{C,a} mod a: its lower density is computable; Erdős's covering theory and the 'density of a union of residue classes' (Rogers/Simpson, and the Hough–Nielsen bound) describe how large a union of classes with distinct moduli can be. Here moduli repeat? (Different C can give the same a: a ≡ −1 mod 4C and mod 4C′ means lcm | a + 1.)
why: If the natural density of the union over all (C, a) with a ≤ A is 1 − o(1) as A → ∞ at a provable rate, then the C-form certifies 'almost all' integers in a quantified way — comparable to Vaughan but elementary; the rate's dependence on the Legendre profile would explain the exceptions.
first_step: Compute lower bound density via Bonferroni for a ≤ A, A = 10³..10⁵; compare with the empirical density of integers ≤ 10⁷ having a C-form certificate with a ≤ A.

title: Why do 409 and 577 fail the C-form? Attempt a T1-style local proof
connection: 409 = 20² + 3², 577 = 24² + 1 = 24² + 1²; both are 'one more than a multiple of a square'? 577 = 576 + 1 = 24² + 1; 409 = 400 + 9; 5569 = 5568 + 1 = ? (5568 = 2⁶·87) no; 9601 = 9600 + 1 = 2⁷·75 + 1 ≈ (98)² = 9604 so 9601 = 98² − 3. 577 = 24² + 1 and 9601 = 98² − 3, 409 = 20² + 9, 5569 = 74² + 93? 74² = 5476, 75² = 5625; so 5569 = 5625 − 56. Hmm no pattern. A local obstruction would be: for all C, every divisor a of 4Cp+1 with a ≡ −1 (4C) violates a Jacobi symbol identity — as in T1 but for specific p. If none exists, the exceptions are 'finite-C accidents' and a certificate exists for some larger C.
why: Either outcome is informative: a new local obstruction at non-squares (contradicting the 'squares only' heuristic for the C-form) or an upper bound on C_min for these primes (so C_min is unbounded in a quantified way).
first_step: Search C up to 10⁶ for p ∈ {409, 577, 5569, 9601} with efficient trial (factor 4Cp+1 via sympy or Pari); if found, record C_min; if not, attempt the Jacobi-symbol argument.

title: Analytic: the C-form expected count Σ_{C ≤ X} E[#{a | 4Cp+1 : a ≡ −1 (4C)}] ≈ Σ_C τ(4Cp+1)/φ(4C) — compare with Type II's Σ_{c,d}
connection: Full Type II has modulus 4cd and N = 4c²dp+1: expected count Σ_{c,d} τ(4c²dp+1)/φ(4cd) — summing over c with fixed d gives an extra log factor (Σ_c 1/φ(4cd) diverges like log). So full Type II has expected count ≍ log p·log²X vs the C-form's log p·log X: the c-parameter is where the extra log in log²p comes from. This explains why the C-form misses some primes (its count is smaller by a log).
why: Quantifies the exceptional-prime phenomenon just observed; and it suggests the (c,d) structure is not decorative: the c-direction provides a *second* log, which is the 'thickness' separating 'almost all' from 'all'? (B3 still says polylog.)
first_step: Compute the expected counts numerically for p ≈ 10⁶ and ranges X ≤ 10³: C-form vs Type II vs Type I; confirm the extra log factor.

title: Mersenne-adjacent: ES for primes p = 2^{2k} + 1 (Fermat primes) and p = (2^m + 1)/3, etc., via explicit factorisations of 4Cp+1
connection: Fermat primes F_k = 2^{2^k} + 1 ≡ 1 mod 4 (hard class? F_k mod 840: F_2 = 17, F_3 = 257 ≡ 257, F_4 = 65537 ≡ 65537 − 78·840 = 17; 17 is not a square mod 840 class... fine). For p = 2^{2k}+1: 4Cp + 1 = C·2^{2k+2} + 4C + 1; for C = 2^{2k}: = 2^{4k+2} + 2^{2k+2} + 1 = (2^{2k+1} + 2^{k+1} + 1)(2^{2k+1} − 2^{k+1} + 1)? (Aurifeuillean-type factorisation of 4x⁴ + 1 style: x⁴ + x² + 1 = (x² + x + 1)(x² − x + 1) with x = 2^{k+1}: 2^{4k+4} + 2^{2k+2} + 1 — close but not equal; adjust.) Explore Aurifeuillean factorisations giving divisors in the right class.
why: Aurifeuillean factorisations are rigid algebraic identities for special p (not polynomial in p but polynomial in the exponent base) — a loophole in Mordell–Schinzel for special prime families.
first_step: For p = 2^{2k} + 1 (k ≤ 20, prime or not), test C ∈ {2^j} for Aurifeuillean factorisations of 4Cp+1 and check residues mod 4C; generalise to p = a^{2k} + 1.

title: Lucas-sequence divisibility: choose C so that 4Cp+1 is a term of a Lucas sequence U_n(P,Q) whose prime divisors are ≡ ±1 mod n (rank of apparition theory)
connection: Primes dividing U_n have rank of apparition dividing n, which forces q ≡ (D/q) mod n — a rigid congruence on divisors! If 4Cp+1 = U_n(P,Q) for some (P,Q,n) with n related to 4C, then every prime divisor q satisfies q ≡ ±1 mod n, and the sign is a Legendre symbol — exactly the kind of 'divisor in a class' rigidity ES needs. The catch: 4Cp+1 must be a Lucas term — a Diophantine coincidence; but with C free and (P,Q) free there are many chances.
why: A concrete (R)-mechanism (rank of apparition) that produces divisors with prescribed residues; the question is coverage.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁴, search C ≤ 10³, Lucas sequences with |P|,|Q| ≤ 5, n ≤ 30 for 4Cp+1 = U_n(P,Q) or V_n(P,Q); check whether the forced residue gives the ES class.

title: Additive combinatorics: the set of C-form certificates for fixed p as a 'multiplicative energy' problem on divisors of {4Cp+1}_C
connection: Writing 4Cp + 1 = ab with a + 1 ≡ b + 1 ≡ 0 (mod 4C): the condition says 4C | gcd(a+1, b+1) and 4C = (ab − 1)/p. So C-form certificates ⟺ pairs (a, b) with (ab − 1)/p dividing both a + 1 and b + 1, and ab ≡ 1 mod p. The set {(a,b): ab ≡ 1 mod p} is the modular hyperbola; we need points on it where the 'height' (ab−1)/p divides a + 1. For a, b ≤ p this forces (ab − 1)/p < p; so it's a question about the modular hyperbola's small-height points with a divisibility — a sum-product-flavoured condition.
why: Sum-product/energy methods (Bourgain–Garaev on modular hyperbolas, Shkredov) give nontrivial pointwise-in-p bounds for incidence-type counts on the hyperbola; they could show the count of (a, b) with the divisibility is ≫ 1 for all p? Unlikely (counts are small) but the hyperbola geometry is the right home for 'why 409 fails'.
first_step: Plot, for p = 409 and a control prime 401, the points (a, b) with ab ≡ 1 mod p, a, b < 4p, colouring those with (ab − 1)/p | gcd(a+1, b+1); see the structural difference.

title: Count the C-form exceptional primes up to X: density → 0 like 1/(log X)^α? or positive density?
connection: If exceptions have positive relative density among primes ≡ 1 mod 24, the C-form is a 'weak' sufficient condition; if they thin out as a power of log, they are the 'tail' and their rate is a measurable analogue of exceptional-set exponents (Vaughan's bound in miniature).
why: Quantifies the gap between C-form and ES; also a test of the 'half-dimensional sieve' heuristics (prediction: exceptions ~ X/(log X)^{1+κ} for the effective sieve dimension κ).
first_step: From the census, fit #exceptions ≤ X vs X/(log X)^β; report β.

title: ES as 'every p has an odd character χ mod 4C and a divisor a of 4Cp+1 with χ(a) = −1 for ALL odd χ' — the character-theoretic restatement of a ≡ −1 (mod 4C)
connection: a ≡ −1 mod 4C ⟺ χ(a) = χ(−1) for all characters χ mod 4C ⟺ χ(a) = −1 for odd χ and +1 for even χ. So the C-form asks for a divisor whose character vector equals that of −1. The 'subgroup relaxation' keeps only one odd character; the full condition is ALL characters. Framing: find (C, a) with χ(a) = χ(−1) ∀χ — a 'complete set of character conditions', the number of which grows with C (φ(4C) conditions), while the number of divisors grows like τ(4Cp+1) ≈ log p on average — the expected number of hits is τ/φ(4C), and Σ_C τ(4Cp+1)/φ(4C) ≈ log p · Σ 1/C → log p · log X. (Same count as before, now seen as 'characters vs divisors'.)
why: The character view suggests a *Fourier-analytic* route: #certificates at C = (1/φ(4C)) Σ_χ χ(−1) Σ_{a | N} χ(a); the χ = trivial term is τ(N)/φ(4C) > 0; the other terms are 'noise' Σ_{a|N} χ(a) = Π_{q^e ∥ N} (1 + χ(q) + … + χ(q)^e). A certificate fails to exist iff the noise exactly cancels the main term. Average over C of the noise — can it be shown to be o(main) at fixed p? That's the M_BM program (B3 says the average main term is only log²p). Record the restatement.
first_step: Write the exact identity and compute, for p = 409 and C ≤ 1000, main vs noise per C to see HOW cancellation happens (is it via single-prime N = q with χ(q) = +1 for all odd χ — i.e. q ≡ 1-type — or via multi-factor cancellations?).

title: Does T1 kill (u, v)-identities? Check what happens to a (u,v)-polynomial identity at p = m² = u² + v²
connection: If an identity in (u,v) valid for all coprime (u,v) with u² + v² ≡ 1 mod 24 existed, it would produce Type I/II solutions for m² whenever m² = u² + v² with gcd(u,v) = 1 and uv ≠ 0 — which happens iff m has a prime factor ≡ 1 mod 4 (Pythagorean). T1 says no such solution exists ⟹ NO (u,v)-polynomial identity can be valid on all coprime (u,v) with the right residues. So (u,v)-identities must also exclude Pythagorean (u,v) — i.e. must depend on more than residues of (u,v). Record as a lemma killing the naive version; the surviving version needs a non-polynomial ingredient (e.g. gcd or primality of u² + v²).
why: Saves a wasted search; and pinpoints the 'Pythagorean' loophole: an identity could be valid only when u² + v² is not a square — but polynomial identities can't 'know' that. Same for u² + 2v², etc. (m² = u² + 2v² has solutions when m has a factor ≡ 1,3 mod 8).
first_step: Write the lemma; then ask: are there identities in (u,v) valid for all (u,v) with u² + v² ≡ 1 mod 24 EXCEPT where u² + v² is a square — impossible for polynomials; so the item above (Gaussian identities) is dead in its polynomial form; keep only residue-branching + non-polynomial variants.

title: Finding: the Type I one-parameter form (c = 1) has its own lone exception below 20000 — p = 2521 ≡ 1 (mod 840) — and certifies all four C-form exceptions
connection: Type I with c = 1: a divisor f of p² + 4d with f ≡ −p (mod 4d). Computation (p < 20000, d < 1500): the only prime ≡ 1 (mod 4) without such a certificate is 2521 (= 3·840 + 1, in the Mordell-hard class 1 mod 840); 409, 577, 5569, 9601 are certified by (d, f) = (11, 75), (5, 3), (17, 7), (67, 851). Conversely 2521 is not a C-form exception. So the two one-parameter forms have disjoint exceptional sets in this range and their union covers everything.
why: Suggests a 'two one-parameter families suffice' phenomenon — ES's structure may be '1 + 1 dimensional' rather than genuinely 2-dimensional; and 2521 becomes the Type I analogue of 409: a hard-class prime where a natural sufficient condition fails for (apparently) local reasons. Both exception types are now concrete test cases for any mechanism.
first_step: Extend both censuses to p ≤ 10⁶; test whether the two exceptional sets stay disjoint (if they ever intersect at a prime p, that p has neither one-parameter certificate — a genuinely '2-parameter' prime); derive the forced reciprocity symbol for Type I c=1 ((−d/f) = 1) and look for the local obstruction at 2521.
alt_first_steps: [free_fable-0284] Compute for p ≤ 20000 the c=1 Type I certificate existence (d ≤ 10⁴); list exceptions; intersect with the C-form exceptions.

connection: Meta-hygiene for the merge: many items across the lanes will silently assume one form; a flag makes it cheap to re-check items when a form turns out weaker than assumed (as happened here).
why: Prevents the C-form confusion from propagating into the merged brainstorm.

title: Visualisation: Ulam-spiral / Klauber-triangle plot of C-form C_min(p) and Type I d_min(p) to spot quadratic-polynomial alignments
connection: Ulam spirals make polynomial families visible as lines; plotting the certificate parameters (or their absence) on a spiral could reveal that exceptions (409, 577, 5569, 9601, 2521) lie on a quadratic curve.
why: Five exceptions is few, but the plot costs nothing and polynomial alignment would be a strong hint toward a Mordell–Schinzel-compatible structure (identities in t with p = Q(t)).
first_step: Generate the plots for p ≤ 10⁶ with colour = log C_min; eyeball; test the exceptional primes against small quadratics.

title: Finite differences in C: Δ_C of the indicator win(p, C) — is the sequence C ↦ win(p, C) 'eventually periodic' or 'quasi-periodic' for fixed p?
connection: For fixed p the C-form win indicator depends on the factorisation of the linear sequence 4Cp+1 — a shifted-prime-factor structure with no periodicity but with 'almost periodicity' in the Besicovitch sense (periodic in C mod q for each small prime q's contribution).
why: If win(p, ·) is Besicovitch almost periodic with a positive mean for every p, then infinitely many C win — pointwise ES with infinitude; the mean's positivity is the question, again — but almost-periodicity theory (Wintner, Schwarz–Spilker) gives a *formula* for the mean as a sum over 'Ramanujan expansions', which might be analysable.
first_step: Compute the Ramanujan–Fourier coefficients of win(p, C) over C ≤ 10⁵ for a few p; check whether the mean (the C-density of winning C) is approximated by the first few terms and is bounded away from 0 across p.

title: Umbral / generating-function identities for the count Σ_C x^C·#{a | 4Cp+1, a ≡ −1 (4C)}: Lambert-series structure
connection: Σ_N τ(N) x^N is a Lambert series; sums restricted to N = 4Cp+1 and a in a class tied to C are 'twisted Lambert series along an AP with varying modulus'. Lambert series have modular transformation properties; perhaps the C-form generating function has a transformation law relating p and 1/p-ish parameters.
why: A transformation law would be a rigid analytic structure (like Zagier's for Σ H(n)q^n). Low-to-medium prior.
first_step: Compute the generating function numerically for small p at |x| < 1 and test for simple transformation behaviour under x → e^{−2πt} ↦ t → 1/(p t)-type substitutions.

title: Hasse-principle-style 'almost local' obstruction for 409 in the shifted form: is there a modulus M such that for every u the condition 'p + u has a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4u' is blocked by p's residue mod M? (A 'uniform local obstruction' — would contradict the belief that only squares are obstructed)
connection: For a fixed u the condition on p is a union of residue classes mod lcm-ish(4u·a); an obstruction for ALL u from a single residue p mod M would mean the C-form fails on an entire AP of primes — plausibly false (Dirichlet + the almost-all results for the C-form). So 409's failure is not an AP obstruction; is it then 'random' (and the C ≤ 60000 search just unlucky — implausible given the expected count Σ_{C ≤ 60000} τ(4·409C+1)/φ(4C) ≈ 52 wins) or a non-AP structural obstruction (like T1, which is a 'square' obstruction — not an AP either)? Expected 66 wins vs 0 observed strongly indicates an obstruction of a new type (not AP, not square).
why: The expected-count argument (≈ 52 expected certificates for 409 with C ≤ 60000 (computed: Σ τ(4·409·C+1)/φ(4C) = 51.8), zero observed) is the sharpest evidence that 409 is structurally obstructed in the C-form; identifying the obstruction type is a genuinely new piece of ES structure.
first_step: Compute the expected count Σ_{C ≤ 60000} τ(4·409·C + 1)/φ(4C) precisely (it is the natural heuristic) and compare with the 0 observed; then test the natural candidate obstruction: for 409, is the forced QNR condition (a/409) = −1 incompatible with a ≡ −1 (mod 4C) and a | 4·409C + 1 for a reason involving 409 ≡ 9 (mod 16) or 409's Gaussian representation 20² + 3²?

title: Gross–Zagier singular moduli factorisation as divisor-structure input
connection: Norms of differences of singular moduli have explicitly known prime factorisations (all primes ≤ D1D2/4) ↔ ES needs divisors of p-tied integers in a class.
why: An integer tied to p with explicitly controlled factorisation (only small primes, with Legendre-symbol constraints) is exactly what the 'class gate' wants.
first_step: Compute N(j(τ_{−4p}) − j(τ_{−3}))-type quantities for small p and check if they produce divisors ≡ −1 mod 4C of 4Cp+1-type integers.

title: Harmonic-mean interpretation: p/4·3 is the harmonic mean of x,y,z
connection: 4/p = 1/x+1/y+1/z ⟺ harmonic mean H(x,y,z) = 3p/4 ↔ means inequalities (H ≤ G ≤ A) give box constraints.
why: Box constraints from mean inequalities are already used; the 'harmonic mean of three integers equals 3p/4' phrasing might connect to integer means literature.
first_step: Search 'integers with prescribed harmonic mean' literature for existence theorems.

title: Intercept form: ES as a plane through the diagonal point — projective dual
connection: Dual: points (1/x,1/y,1/z) of the plane X+Y+Z = 4/p with unit-fraction coordinates ↔ rational points on a plane with all coordinates reciprocals of integers.
why: Duality may bring Schmidt subspace theorem-type tools (points of small height on planes with coordinates of special form).
first_step: Record the dual formulation and check whether Schmidt-subspace-type results bound the number of solutions in a way that conflicts with zero (no: they give upper bounds) — note as calibration.

title: GPU kernel for (★)/I3 census to 10^12
connection: Repo census to 10^10 single engine ↔ GPU acceleration for residue-filter checks.
why: Extends CERTIFIED data for I3_𝒞 and (★) failures; tests growth of least u.
